tracks.name: Django Foundations
tracks.description: Create a project, connect URLs, write views, and render templates.

lessons.title: 1. Projects and apps
lessons.summary: A project holds settings and URLs; each app is a focused bundle of models, views, and migrations.

activities.title: Two commands, two scopes
activities.instruction: `django-admin startproject config .` creates the project: settings, root URLs, and `manage.py`. `python manage.py startapp blog` creates one app. Django only loads an app's models and templates after the app is listed in `INSTALLED_APPS`.
activities.example:
django-admin startproject config .
python manage.py startapp blog

# config/settings.py
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    # ...Django's own apps...
    'blog',
]

activities.title: What does startapp create?
activities.question: What does `python manage.py startapp blog` create?
choices: An app package with models, views, tests, and a migrations folder
activities.answer: An app package with models, views, tests, and a migrations folder
activities.explanation: An app is Python code. Its tables appear later, when you write models and run `migrate`.

activities.title: Register the blog app
activities.instruction: Add `'blog'` to `INSTALLED_APPS` so Django loads the app's models and templates.

teaching.text: A Django project is the whole site: settings, database configuration, root URLconf, and `manage.py`. An app is a reusable slice of that site, such as `blog` or `accounts`.

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    'django.contrib.admin',
    'django.contrib.auth',
    'django.contrib.contenttypes',
    'django.contrib.sessions',
    'django.contrib.messages',
    'django.contrib.staticfiles',
    'blog',
]
Forgetting to register an app causes confusing errors: its models are not discovered, and its templates may not be found.

lessons.task: Add `'blog'` to `INSTALLED_APPS` so Django loads the app.
lessons.starterCode:
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    'django.contrib.admin',
    'django.contrib.auth',
    'django.contrib.contenttypes',
    'django.contrib.sessions',
    'django.contrib.messages',
    'django.contrib.staticfiles',
    # Register the blog app here
]
hints: Add the app's import name, `'blog'`, as a string in the list.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does each app keep its own models, migrations, and templates instead of one giant shared folder?

lessons.title: 2. Your first view
lessons.summary: A view is a Python callable that receives a request and returns a response.

activities.title: Request in, response out
activities.instruction: Every view takes an `HttpRequest` and returns an `HttpResponse`. `HttpResponse` writes the body directly; templates and JSON are built on top of it.

activities.title: What must a view return?
activities.question: What must a Django view return?
choices: An HttpResponse, or raise an exception
activities.answer: An HttpResponse, or raise an exception
activities.explanation: A dictionary is context for a template, not a response. A view must produce something the HTTP layer can send, or raise an exception such as `Http404`.

activities.title: Write a health view
activities.instruction: Write a view named `health` that accepts `request` and returns the plain text `ok`.

teaching.text: The request object carries the method, headers, query string, body, and user. The response carries the status, headers, and body. Everything else in Django is a way of building one from the other.
Views live in `views.py` by convention, but Django only needs an importable function. URLconf decides which URL calls it.

lessons.starterCode:
from django.http import HttpResponse

# Add a view named health here
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does Django pass a request object to every view, even when this view ignores it?

lessons.title: 3. URL routing
lessons.summary: URLconf maps a path to a view, and include() forwards a prefix to an app's own routes.

activities.title: Project routes, app routes
activities.instruction: The project URLconf handles site-wide prefixes. `include('blog.urls')` delegates everything after `blog/` to the app, which keeps app routes portable.
activities.example:
# config/urls.py
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import include, path

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('blog/', include('blog.urls')),
]

# blog/urls.py
from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path('', views.post_list, name='post_list'),
]

activities.title: What does include do?
activities.question: What does `include('blog.urls')` do?
choices: Forwards paths beginning with `blog/` to the app's URLconf
activities.answer: Forwards paths beginning with `blog/` to the app's URLconf
activities.explanation: `include()` composes URLconfs. The prefix is stripped before the app's patterns are matched, so the app does not hardcode its mount point.

activities.title: Wire the blog app
activities.instruction: Add the `blog/` prefix to the project URLconf and point the app root at `views.post_list`.

teaching.text: Django tries patterns in order and stops at the first match. Put specific routes before catch-all patterns, and give each route a `name` so templates can build URLs without hardcoding them.

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('blog/', include('blog.urls')),
]

# blog/urls.py
urlpatterns = [
    path('', views.post_list, name='post_list'),
]
Trailing slashes matter. `blog/` and `blog` are different URLs unless `APPEND_SLASH` redirects one to the other.

lessons.task: Wire `blog/` to the app URLconf and the app root to `views.post_list`.
lessons.starterCode:
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import include, path

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    # Add the blog routes here
]
lessons.solution:
# config/urls.py
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import include, path

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('blog/', include('blog.urls')),
]

# blog/urls.py
from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path('', views.post_list, name='post_list'),
]
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is `include()` better than listing every app route in the project URLconf?

lessons.title: 4. Templates
lessons.summary: render() combines the request, a template, and a context dictionary into an HTML response.

activities.title: Build HTML from data
activities.instruction: `render()` loads the template, evaluates its tags against the context, and returns an `HttpResponse`. The context is a normal dictionary keyed by the names the template uses.

activities.title: Autoescaping
activities.question: A post title contains `<script>alert(1)</script>`. What does `{{ post.title }}` render?
choices: Escaped text that displays the markup safely
activities.answer: Escaped text that displays the markup safely
activities.explanation: Django autoescapes variables by default. Use `|safe` only on trusted HTML, never on user input.

activities.title: Render a list page
activities.instruction: Return `blog/index.html` with the posts available as `posts`.

teaching.text: Templates keep presentation out of Python. The view fetches and prepares data; the template loops, formats, and escapes it. `APP_DIRS: True` lets Django find each app's `templates/` folder.
Template paths inside an app include the app name: `blog/templates/blog/index.html`. That namespacing prevents two apps from silently overriding each other.

lessons.task: Render `blog/index.html` with the posts available as `posts`.
lessons.starterCode:
from django.shortcuts import render
from .models import Post

def post_list(request):
    posts = Post.objects.order_by('-created_at')
    # Return the template with posts in the context
hints: Call `render` with the request, the template path, and a context dictionary.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why should the view pass a queryset instead of building an HTML string in Python?

tracks.name: Models & the ORM
tracks.description: Describe data once, migrate it, query it, and validate user input.

lessons.title: 5. Models and migrations
lessons.summary: A model class describes a table; migrations record how that description changes over time.

activities.title: A class that becomes a table
activities.instruction: Each field becomes a column. `makemigrations` compares the model to the migration history and writes a migration file; `migrate` applies it to the database.
activities.example:
from django.db import models

class Post(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    slug = models.SlugField(unique=True)
    body = models.TextField()
    published = models.BooleanField(default=False)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

    def __str__(self):
        return self.title

# python manage.py makemigrations
# python manage.py migrate

activities.title: Which command writes the file?
activities.question: Which command writes a new migration file?
activities.explanation: `makemigrations` writes the plan; `migrate` applies it. Keeping them separate lets you review schema changes before touching the database.

activities.title: Model a blog post
activities.instruction: Define a `Post` model with a title, slug, body, published flag, and an auto-set created_at timestamp.

teaching.text: Models are the single source of truth for your data shape. Django derives forms, the admin, and SQL from them, so field types and constraints are worth getting right the first time.

class Post(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    slug = models.SlugField(unique=True)
    body = models.TextField()
    published = models.BooleanField(default=False)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
Commit migrations with the code that needs them. Recreating the database from models hides drift that will break the next deploy.

lessons.task: Define a `Post` model with the five fields described in the lesson.
lessons.starterCode:
from django.db import models

# Define the Post model here
hints: A model is a class that inherits from `models.Model`.
Use `CharField` for title, `SlugField` for slug, `TextField` for body, `BooleanField` for published, and `DateTimeField` for created_at.
lessons.solution:
from django.db import models

class Post(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    slug = models.SlugField(unique=True)
    body = models.TextField()
    published = models.BooleanField(default=False)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

    def __str__(self):
        return self.title
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why should migrations live in version control instead of rebuilding the database from models on every machine?

lessons.title: 6. Querying with the ORM
lessons.summary: The ORM turns Python method calls into SQL and returns model instances or querysets.

activities.title: Build a queryset lazily
activities.instruction: `filter()` returns a lazy queryset: the SQL runs when you iterate, slice, or evaluate it. `get()` is for exactly one row and raises `DoesNotExist` or `MultipleObjectsReturned`.
activities.example:
published = Post.objects.filter(published=True).order_by('-created_at')
latest = published.first()
post = Post.objects.get(slug='hello-django')
count = Post.objects.filter(published=True).count()

activities.title: When get finds two rows
activities.question: `Post.objects.get(published=True)` matches three rows. What happens?
choices: It returns a queryset of three rows
activities.explanation: `get()` promises exactly one row. Use `filter()` plus `first()` when several rows are valid.

activities.title: Query published posts
activities.instruction: Build a queryset of published posts, newest first.

teaching.text: Field lookups are keyword arguments: `title__icontains`, `created_at__gte`, `author__username`. Django composes them into one SQL query, so keep filtering in the database rather than in Python loops.

Post.objects.filter(published=True).order_by('-created_at')
Post.objects.filter(title__icontains='django')
Post.objects.filter(created_at__year=2026)
Each item access can trigger another query. Use `select_related()` for foreign keys and `prefetch_related()` for many-to-many relations to avoid N+1 queries.

lessons.task: Build a queryset of published posts ordered newest first.
lessons.starterCode:
from .models import Post

# Query published posts, newest first
hints: Chain `.order_by('-created_at')`; the leading minus means descending.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is filtering in the ORM usually better than loading every row and filtering in Python?

lessons.title: 7. Relationships
lessons.summary: A ForeignKey links rows, and related_name gives the reverse side a readable name.

activities.title: Posts belong to an author
activities.instruction: `ForeignKey` stores the related row's primary key. `on_delete` decides what happens when that row is deleted, and `related_name` names the reverse accessor.
activities.example:
class Author(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=120)

class Post(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    author = models.ForeignKey(
        Author,
        on_delete=models.CASCADE,
        related_name='posts',
    )

# author.posts.all()
# post.author.name

activities.title: CASCADE deletes
activities.question: A post uses `on_delete=models.CASCADE`. What happens when its author is deleted?
choices: The post keeps a null author
Django refuses to delete the author
activities.explanation: CASCADE deletes dependent rows. Use `PROTECT` when losing the parent should be blocked, or `SET_NULL` with `null=True` when the child should survive.

activities.title: Link posts to authors
activities.instruction: Add an `author` ForeignKey to `Post` with CASCADE deletion and the reverse name `posts`.

teaching.text: Relationships are part of the schema, not an afterthought. Choose the delete behaviour deliberately: CASCADE for owned data, PROTECT for important references, SET_NULL for optional links.

author = models.ForeignKey(
    Author,
    on_delete=models.CASCADE,
    related_name='posts',
)
Without `related_name`, the reverse accessor is `post_set`. A clear name like `posts` reads better in templates and queries.

lessons.task: Add an `author` ForeignKey with CASCADE and `related_name='posts'`.
lessons.starterCode:
from django.db import models

class Post(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    # Add the author relationship here
hints: A ForeignKey takes the related model first, then `on_delete` and `related_name`.
lessons.solution:
from django.db import models

class Post(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    author = models.ForeignKey(
        Author,
        on_delete=models.CASCADE,
        related_name='posts',
    )
lessons.reflectionPrompt: When would `PROTECT` be a better choice than `CASCADE` for a foreign key?

lessons.title: 8. Forms and validation
lessons.summary: A ModelForm validates request data and saves a model instance in one step.

activities.title: Bind, validate, save
activities.instruction: Binding a form to `request.POST` lets it validate that data. `is_valid()` runs field and model validation; only then should you call `save()`.

activities.title: What is_valid does
activities.question: What does `form.is_valid()` do?
choices: Saves the object to the database
Runs validation, fills cleaned_data, and returns True or False
activities.answer: Runs validation, fills cleaned_data, and returns True or False
activities.explanation: Validation and saving are separate steps. `save()` is safe only after `is_valid()` returns True.

activities.title: Handle a create form
activities.instruction: Bind `PostForm` to `request.POST`, validate it, save on success, and render the empty form otherwise.

teaching.text: A `ModelForm` derives fields and validation from the model. Override `clean_<field>()` for extra rules, and use `fields = [...]` to avoid exposing sensitive model fields.
Every POST form needs `{% csrf_token %}` in the template. Django rejects POST requests without a valid CSRF token.

lessons.task: Bind, validate, and save a `PostForm` from `request.POST`.
lessons.starterCode:
from django.shortcuts import render
from .forms import PostForm

def create_post(request):
    # Handle POST, then fall back to an empty form
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is it unsafe to save a form before checking `is_valid()`?

tracks.name: Views, APIs & Production
tracks.description: Accept input, reuse generic views, expose JSON, and ship with safe settings.

lessons.title: 9. Request data and 404s
lessons.summary: Read query parameters with defaults and turn a missing row into a clean 404.

activities.title: Search, then look up
activities.instruction: `request.GET.get('q', '')` returns a string or the default. `get_object_or_404` fetches one row or raises `Http404`, which Django renders as a 404 page.

activities.title: Missing query key
activities.question: What does `request.GET.get('q')` return when the URL has no `q` parameter?
activities.explanation: `.get()` returns None when the key is absent. Pass a second argument, such as `''` or `'0'`, when the rest of the code expects a string.

activities.title: Search posts by title
activities.instruction: Read `q` with an empty-string default and filter post titles case-insensitively.

teaching.text: Path parameters identify a resource; query parameters tune a collection. Both arrive as strings, so parse numbers explicitly and clamp pagination values before using them.

q = request.GET.get('q', '')
page = max(1, int(request.GET.get('page', 1)))
posts = Post.objects.filter(title__icontains=q)
`get_object_or_404` is the honest default for detail pages. Returning a 200 with an empty object makes a missing resource look like a successful one.

lessons.task: Read `q` with a default and filter titles case-insensitively.
lessons.starterCode:
from django.shortcuts import render
from .models import Post

def search(request):
    # Read q and filter post titles
hints: `request.GET.get('q', '')` gives you a string even when the parameter is missing.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why should a page that takes `?page=` defend against zero, negative, and non-numeric values?

lessons.title: 10. Class-based views
lessons.summary: Generic views package the list and detail patterns behind class attributes.

activities.title: Attributes instead of boilerplate
activities.instruction: `ListView` fetches a queryset and puts it in the context. `DetailView` fetches one object by `pk` or `slug`. Override methods only when the defaults do not fit.
activities.example:
from django.views.generic import DetailView, ListView
from .models import Post

class PostListView(ListView):
    model = Post
    template_name = 'blog/post_list.html'
    context_object_name = 'posts'

class PostDetailView(DetailView):
    model = Post
    template_name = 'blog/post_detail.html'
    context_object_name = 'post'

activities.title: Which attribute selects the data?
activities.question: Which `ListView` attribute tells it which model to query?
activities.explanation: `model` drives the default queryset. `template_name` chooses the HTML, and `context_object_name` names the list in the template.

activities.title: Build a post list view
activities.instruction: Create `PostListView` using `ListView`, with model `Post`, template `blog/post_list.html`, and context name `posts`.

teaching.text: Class-based views are ordinary Python classes with mixins for HTTP methods. They remove repetition, but a short function view is still the clearer choice for one-off logic.
Override `get_queryset()` to filter, not `get()`: the built-in `get()` already handles the response and 404.

lessons.task: Create a `PostListView` with the model, template, and context name set.
lessons.starterCode:
from django.views.generic import ListView
from .models import Post

# Create PostListView here
lessons.solution:
from django.views.generic import ListView
from .models import Post

class PostListView(ListView):
    model = Post
    template_name = 'blog/post_list.html'
    context_object_name = 'posts'
lessons.reflectionPrompt: When is a function view easier to read than a class-based view?

lessons.title: 11. JSON APIs with DRF
lessons.summary: Django REST Framework serializes models and validates JSON in both directions.

activities.title: One serializer, two directions
activities.instruction: A serializer turns model instances into JSON for responses and validates incoming JSON for writes. `many=True` serializes a queryset; `raise_exception=True` turns invalid input into a 400 response.

activities.title: Why not dump the model?
activities.question: Why use a serializer instead of `json.dumps(post.__dict__)`?
choices: They choose exposed fields and validate incoming data
Django models cannot be converted to JSON at all
activities.answer: They choose exposed fields and validate incoming data
activities.explanation: `__dict__` leaks internal fields and accepts anything. A serializer defines the public contract and checks writes before they reach the database.

activities.title: Serialize posts
activities.instruction: Create a `PostSerializer` for `Post` and return published posts from `PostList.get`.

teaching.text: DRF adds serializers, request parsing, authentication, permissions, and browsable responses. Add `'rest_framework'` to `INSTALLED_APPS` and keep the API surface explicit with `fields`.
Never use `fields = '__all__'` on a model with ownership or private fields. List the fields the client is allowed to see and change.

lessons.task: Add a `PostSerializer` and return published posts as JSON.
lessons.starterCode:
from rest_framework import serializers
from rest_framework.response import Response
from rest_framework.views import APIView
from .models import Post

# Add PostSerializer and PostList.get
hints: A `ModelSerializer` needs a nested `Meta` with `model` and `fields`.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Which fields should never be writable through a public serializer, even if they exist on the model?

lessons.title: 12. Admin and production settings
lessons.summary: The admin gives you a working back office; production settings keep it from leaking internals.

activities.title: Register the model, harden the site
activities.instruction: `admin.site.register()` exposes a model in the built-in admin. In production, `DEBUG` must be off, `SECRET_KEY` must come from the environment, and `ALLOWED_HOSTS` must list the domains Django will answer for.
activities.example:
# blog/admin.py
from django.contrib import admin
from .models import Post

class PostAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    list_display = ('title', 'published', 'created_at')

admin.site.register(Post, PostAdmin)

# config/settings.py
import os

DEBUG = False
SECRET_KEY = os.environ['DJANGO_SECRET_KEY']
ALLOWED_HOSTS = os.environ.get('DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS', '').split(',')

activities.title: Why DEBUG must be off
activities.question: Why must `DEBUG` be `False` in production?
choices: Debug pages expose settings, SQL, source paths, and tracebacks
The admin refuses to load otherwise
activities.answer: Debug pages expose settings, SQL, source paths, and tracebacks
activities.explanation: A production traceback can reveal secrets and internal structure. With DEBUG off, Django returns a generic 500 page and logs the details server-side.

activities.title: Register the model and harden settings
activities.instruction: Register `Post` in the admin and set `DEBUG = False` with the allowed hosts read from the environment.

teaching.text: The admin is a staff-only CRUD interface generated from your models. It is powerful, so protect it with strong accounts, HTTPS, and access controls instead of leaving it at `/admin/` with a weak password.

DEBUG = False
SECRET_KEY = os.environ['DJANGO_SECRET_KEY']
ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['example.com', 'www.example.com']
CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS = ['https://example.com']
Run `python manage.py check --deploy` before shipping. It flags missing HTTPS, cookie, HSTS, and secret-key settings that are easy to forget.

class PostAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
